item.title: USA Today Sues OpenAI for Over $250 Million Over Copyright Infringement
item.description:
USA Today Sues OpenAI for Over $250 Million Over Copyright Infringement

USA Today Co., together with several local newspapers it owns, has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI alleging that the AI company copied “hundreds of thousands” of articles to train its models.

🔍 Overview

  • USA Today is the latest publisher to sue OpenAI.
  • The lawsuit seeks damages of more than $250 million.
  • The filing claims OpenAI’s use of the content has caused “real and continuing” harm to the outlets.

⚖️ Legal Claims

  • OpenAI allegedly did not ask for permission to use USA Today’s articles.
  • The plaintiff asserts OpenAI “took” the content to build products worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
  • The complaint states that OpenAI’s commercial success rests on large‑scale copyright infringement.
  • The core allegation is that OpenAI copied hundreds of thousands of articles for training its AI models.

📄 Parties Involved

  • Plaintiff: USA Today Co. (including its local newspapers)
  • Local outlets named in the suit: The Tennessean, Indy Star, The Columbus Dispatch, The Oklahoman, and several others.
  • Other publishers currently suing OpenAI:
    • The New York Times
    • The Intercept
    • CNET owner Ziff Davis
    • CBC/Radio‑Canada
    • Encyclopaedia Britannica
    • Merriam‑Webster
    • The Seattle Times
    • A coalition of nearly 400 local newspapers

📈 Why It Matters

  • The case adds to a growing string of copyright lawsuits against OpenAI.
  • Plaintiffs argue that the alleged infringement harms the news industry’s ability to monetize content.
  • OpenAI has not responded to a request for comment from The Verge.

The outcome could influence how AI developers source and use copyrighted material.

#OpenAI #CopyrightLaw #MediaLawsuits

Source: USA Today becomes the latest publisher to sue OpenAI

item.title: German Arbitration Law Faces Growing AI Guidance but No Formal Rules Yet
item.description:
German Arbitration Law Faces Growing AI Guidance but No Formal Rules Yet

If you are looking for specific legislation or institutional guidance to tell you whether artificial intelligence (AI) belongs in your arbitration in Germany, you can stop waiting.

🔍 Overview

  • German law does not contain explicit AI provisions in the German Code of Civil Procedure (ZPO), but existing provisions already answer the key questions.
  • The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) adds additional requirements that will increasingly apply to arbitration.
  • Several arbitration institutions have issued AI‑related guidelines, while the German Institution of Arbitration (DIS) has not yet published specific rules.

📜 Legal Framework

  • ZPO Structure: Sections 1025 et seq. are built around a personally appointed human arbitrator; section 1036(1) refers to the “person” offered the arbitrator position; section 1054 requires the award to bear the arbitrators’ signatures – a formal act only a natural person can perform.
  • Case Law: The Federal Court of Justice (12 January 2023, I ZB 41/22) set aside an award where the appointed arbitrator did not participate, confirming that delegation of the decision‑making function to an AI tool would breach the mandatory participation requirement.
  • Public‑policy Ground: Delegating the substantive decision to AI may also trigger the procedural public‑policy ground under section 1059(2) no. 2(b) ZPO.
  • Lawyer Duties: German lawyers must practise conscientiously (BRAO § 43) and must not knowingly disseminate untruths (BRAO § 43a(3) sentence 2), which bars the intentional use of fabricated AI‑generated authorities.

🏛️ Institutional Guidance

Institution AI Guidance Published Year
SVAMC AI Guidelines 2024 (April)
SCC AI Guide 2024 (October)
CIArb AI Guideline & Template Procedural Order 2025
VIAC AI Notes 2025
CIETAC AI Notes 2025
ICC Task force on AI (no guidance yet) –
  • The DIS has engaged in the debate through events, a cooperation with the SVAMC announced in December 2025, and a joint submission with 15 other institutions to the European Commission on high‑risk AI classification.
  • The DIS has not published any specific AI rules or practice note.

⚖️ Key Principles Across Institutions

  • Arbitral tribunals must not delegate their decision‑making powers to AI.
  • Counsel remain responsible for the accuracy of factual and legal submissions.
  • All participants must ensure AI tools comply with applicable confidentiality obligations.

🚧 Current Gaps & Recent Developments

  • 2026 ZPO Reform Bill (adopted 10 June 2026) modernises arbitration (video hearings, electronic awards) but does not address AI tools.
  • The same omission appears in state‑court litigation where the ZPO also lacks AI‑specific provisions.
  • The DIS’s joint submission to the European Commission asks for a distinction between AI used in adjudicative functions and AI used for administrative case management.

💡 Practical Implications for Practitioners

  • No Delegation: An arbitrator who outsources the substance of a decision to an AI tool no longer participates in the act of deciding, risking set‑aside of the award.
  • Right to be Heard: Simply uploading written submissions to a large language model does not satisfy the procedural right to be heard.
  • Professional Conduct: Lawyers must avoid presenting AI‑generated fabricated authorities, as this would breach the duty under the BRAO.
  • Technology‑Friendly Rules: The 2018 DIS Rules already support electronic communication (article 4.1) and the discussion of IT‑based efficiency measures (article 27.4(i) and Annex 3), providing a procedural basis for careful AI use.

The landscape shows a rapid emergence of institutional guidance on AI in arbitration, yet German arbitration law itself remains silent on the matter, leaving practitioners to rely on existing ZPO provisions, professional duties, and emerging best‑practice notes.

#Arbitration #AIRegulation #GermanLaw #EUAIAct

Source: AI in arbitration: Germany’s missing rulebook is nothing to worry about | Freshfields

item.title: Sen. Schiff pushes for AI regulatory agency amid White House non‑binding pledge
item.description:
Sen. Schiff pushes for AI regulatory agency amid White House non‑binding pledge

In 2026, Senator Adam Schiff highlighted a growing push for federal regulation of artificial intelligence, citing recent White House events and a Supreme Court decision that could shape any new AI agency.

🔍 Overview

  • President Donald Trump gathered AI CEOs at the White House to sign a non‑binding pact agreeing to keep AI safe.
  • A separate group of tech executives signed a voluntary pledge to evaluate their own AI systems.
  • Schiff, a Democrat from California, opened the conversation by discussing self‑dealing and corruption in politics.
  • He emphasized the need for regulation rather than relying solely on industry promises.

🏛️ Legal backdrop

  • The Supreme Court case Loper Bright overturned a Reagan‑era precedent that gave agencies deference when laws were vague (Chevron deference).
  • Courts now decide on such matters, which could cause any new AI regulation to become entangled in litigation.

⚙️ Proposed regulatory approach

  • Schiff supports creating a new agency to regulate AI.
  • He noted that the Supreme Court decision makes immediate litigation a real risk for new regulations.

🚨 National security concerns

  • Advanced models, especially those that improve themselves recursively, reduce our ability to understand their decisions.
  • The Pentagon’s unbridled AI use could lead to calamities; there is a call to investigate AI’s role in the bombing of an Iranian girls’ school.
  • Anthropic has refused to use AI for domestic mass surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, prompting an administration effort to “kill” the company.
  • When asked about these concerns, the president answered that the world need not worry because “these companies love America.”

📣 Why it matters

  • The combination of industry self‑regulation, a potential new federal agency, and a Supreme Court shift creates a complex landscape for AI governance.
  • National security implications add urgency to establishing clear, enforceable rules.

#AIRegulation #SenSchiff #NationalSecurity #SupremeCourt

Source: Sen. Adam Schiff on making Congress relevant in the AI age

item.title: Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act Introduced in Congress
item.description:
Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act Introduced in Congress

Senator Bernie Sanders (I‑VT) and Representative Greg Casar (D‑TX) have introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would prohibit the development of artificial superintelligence and pause advanced AI systems.

🔍 Overview

  • The bill defines artificial superintelligence as technology capable of the “destruction or disempowerment of humanity,” including overthrowing the government.
  • It also pauses development of “frontier models,” which lawmakers classify as advanced AI systems trained on a specific data threshold.

⚙️ How the Bill Works

  • A scientist‑led Department of Artificial Intelligence would be created to oversee the technology.
  • AI companies must obtain permission from this department before developing advanced AI models.
  • The department would monitor frontier AI models, remove dangerous features, and supervise the destruction of artificial superintelligence.
  • Development of advanced AI could resume only after the department is established.

⚖️ Penalties

  • AI leaders who violate the law could face up to 20 years in prison.
  • The same penalty applies to “rogue actors” who break the rules but are not employed by an AI company.
  • The penalty is described as “similar to existing penalties related to unlawfully developing nuclear weapons.”

📊 Context

  • A former Anthropic researcher warned there is more than a 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” by the end of the decade.
  • Last week, California Governor Gavin Newsom proposed a “kill switch” for frontier models.

#AIRegulation #ArtificialSuperintelligence #USLegislation

Source: Bernie Sanders proposes banning ‘superintelligence’ and putting violators in prison

item.title: New Mexico Supreme Court Fines Lawyer for AI-Generated Brief with Fake Testimony
item.description:
New Mexico Supreme Court Fines Lawyer for AI-Generated Brief with Fake Testimony

The New Mexico Supreme Court has penalized lawyer Stephen Aarons for submitting an appeal for a client’s murder conviction that contained AI-fabricated witnesses and false police testimony.

⚙️ Key details

In a Wednesday filing, the court held Stephen Aarons in contempt and issued a $5,000 fine for failing to “verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief.”

  • Fabrications: The brief included false testimony from “wholly fabricated witnesses” and false testimony regarding the appearance and clothing of the shooter.
  • Tool Used: Aarons admitted to using ChatGPT, stating he believed it would produce a “bulletproof summary” of the trial.
  • Court Response: Justice C. Shannon Bacon questioned Aarons’ awareness of AI risks, noting that the problem of lawyers relying on “AI hallucinations” is an “above-the-fold story every single day.”
  • Defense: In a statement to Reuters, Aarons said, “I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake.”

💡 Why it matters

This incident follows other legal cases involving AI-generated inaccuracies:

Party Involved Issue
Two unnamed law firms Submitted a brief with “numerous false, inaccurate, and misleading legal citations and quotations”
Lawyers for Mike Lindell Fined for including fake AI citations and AI-generated misquotes in a brief

#ChatGPT #LegalTech #AIHallucinations #NewMexico

Source: Lawyer fined $5K over AI-hallucinated witnesses in a murder case
